sources_and_qualifications: PARTIAL SUPPORT; phenotype details still require species-matched confirmation. Partha et al. (2017), eLife 6:e25884, https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.25884: reports subcutaneous eyes for Nannospalax and includes N. galili; use morphological background, not gene-loss results, for coding. Related-taxon anatomical evidence: Sanyal et al. (1990), The eye of the blind mole rat, Spalax ehrenbergi. Rudiment with hidden function?, IOVS 31:1398-1404, PMID 2142147, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2142147/. Historical S. ehrenbergi is not automatically species-identical to N. galili; species-specific absence of image formation and circadian entrainment not independently verified here. Existing codes preserved, not blanket-approved.

MORPHOLOGICAL SUPPORT; Partha et al. (2017), eLife 6:e25884, https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.25884: describes subcutaneous eyes in this species and cites the original anatomy. Primary anatomical source located: Sweet G (1909), The Eyes of Chrysochloris hottentota and C. asiatica, Quarterly Journal of Microscopical Science 53:327-338, https://field.biodiversitylibrary.org/part/201079 (full original not inspected). Vestigial anatomy does not alone quantify residual photoreception. Fossoriality threshold still requires an explicit definition.

eye_morphology_evidence: direct ultrastructure does not settle the state
sources_and_qualifications: REVIEW EYE_STATE 2; Grim N (1990), Whorl-Like Outer Segments in the Retina of the Mole (Scalopus aquaticus), Acta Anatomica 138:261-264, https://doi.org/10.1159/000146949; PMID 2389672. Direct ultrastructure study reports abnormal outer-segment morphology and sensory cells consistent with functional receptors. Does not establish absence of image-forming vision or validate the supplied skin/fused-lid description. Eye-state 2 remains unresolved pending an operational definition and additional anatomy; source column update does not approve this code or independently verify ecology.

MORPHOLOGICAL SUPPORT; Partha et al. (2017), eLife 6:e25884, https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.25884: describes small eyes with thick eyelids and activity above and below ground. Its cited species source: Catania KC (1999), A nose that looks like a hand and acts like an eye: the unusual mechanosensory system of the star-nosed mole, J Comp Physiol A 185:367-372, PMID 10555270, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10555270/ (primary source located; eye-specific support taken from Partha introduction). Eye-state 1 is consistent with reduction, not proof of absent image formation. Review fossoriality 2 if defined as obligate subterranean rather than burrow-dwelling.

DIRECT VISUAL EVIDENCE; Hetling et al. (2005), Features of visual function in the naked mole-rat Heterocephalus glaber, PMID 15647925, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15647925/: anatomical and physiological assays support small eyes and attenuated retinal responses. Nikitina et al. (2004), Postnatal development of the eye in the naked mole rat, https://doi.org/10.1002/ar.a.20025, PMID 15052660. Crish et al. (2006), Central visual system of the naked mole-rat, https://doi.org/10.1002/ar.a.20288, PMID 16419086. Supports reduced visual apparatus with retained photic responses; does not imply normal image-forming acuity. Record morphology and function separately.

PARTIAL DIRECT SUPPORT; The role of ambient temperature and light as cues in the control of circadian rhythms of Damaraland mole-rat (2024), Chronobiology International, https://doi.org/10.1080/07420528.2024.2325649, PMID 38444071: species-specific experimental light/temperature effects on locomotor rhythms; does not measure image-forming acuity. Species background: Adaptations to a subterranean environment and longevity revealed by the analysis of mole rat genomes (2014), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4350764/. Precise eye-state 1 and poor-acuity claim require additional species-specific anatomy/behaviour; do not infer the phenotype from the genomic outcome being tested.

image_forming_vision_evidence: direct (reduced spatial resolution, retained central projections)
sources_and_qualifications: DIRECT SPECIES-MATCHED ANATOMY; Herbin M, Reperant J, Cooper HM (1994), Visual system of the fossorial mole-lemmings, Ellobius talpinus and Ellobius lutescens, J Comp Neurol 346:253-275, https://doi.org/10.1002/cne.903460206; PMID 7962718. E. talpinus eye axial length 2.9 mm; reduced spatial resolution and retained central visual projections. Retain eye-state 1 as a provisional anatomical interpretation; do not recode to 0 for power and do not equate anatomical reduction with blindness. Existing Extended Data grouping is an analysis decision, not an independent phenotype source.

DIRECT ECOLOGY ONLY; Lacey et al. (1997), Burrow Sharing by Colonial Tuco-Tucos (Ctenomys sociabilis), J Mammal 78:556-562, https://doi.org/10.2307/1382907: field capture/radiotelemetry supports residence in shared burrow systems. Does not validate eye-state 0, normal acuity, or the precise surface-foraging sentence. Related-species anatomy only: Vega-Zuniga et al. (2017), Selective binocular vision loss in two subterranean caviomorph rodents: Spalacopus cyanus and Ctenomys talarum, https://doi.org/10.1038/srep41704. C. talarum is not C. sociabilis; do not use as direct species validation. Eye-state 0 remains unverified; define whether occasional surface activity is allowed in fossoriality 2. | CONTINUED SEARCH (2 Nov 2026): no species-matched eye study found. Related species only: C. talarum and C. magellanicus have normally developed eyes, relatively low photoreceptor density with a high cone proportion, and UV-tuned S opsin (J Comp Neurol 2010; https://ri.conicet.gov.ar/handle/11336/96381; https://scicrunch.org/20737597). Not transferred to C. sociabilis; states remain unknown.

SPECIES-MATCHED RETINAL SOURCE; Mass AM, Supin AYa (1989), Distribution of ganglion cells in the retina of an Amazon river dolphin Inia geoffrensis, Aquatic Mammals 15(2):49-56, https://www.aquaticmammalsjournal.org/wp-content/uploads/2009/12/Mass.pdf (publisher source located; full PDF access blocked). Author review: Mass and Supin (2007), Adaptive features of aquatic mammals eye, https://doi.org/10.1002/ar.20529, describes small eyes and retinal topography in Inia. Supports retained visual apparatus; eye-state 1 remains an interpretation requiring a comparative reduction criterion, not a blind state. A river dolphin is aquatic, not a terrestrial surface-dweller; fossoriality 0 must mean non-burrowing. | CONTINUED SEARCH (2 Nov 2026): no further species-matched evidence found in this round.

eye_morphology_evidence: direct retina organised; reduction not validated
sources_and_qualifications: DIRECT RETINAL ANATOMY; Retina of river dolphin Lipotes Vexillifer (1983), PMID 6857230, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6857230/: reports an organised ten-layer retina and ganglion-cell organisation. Supports retained retinal structure; does not alone validate greatly reduced eyes, measured poor acuity or eye-state 1 against a specified comparator. Retain code as provisional until additional evidence and definitions are supplied. Fossoriality 0 must mean non-burrowing, not terrestrial surface habitat. | CONTINUED SEARCH (2 Nov 2026): secondary species account (Duke OBIS-SEAMAP, https://seamap.env.duke.edu/species/180409/html) describes small, functional eyes and apparently poor vision; secondary, no measured comparator. Eye morphology remains unresolved.

DIRECT BEHAVIOUR WITH LIMITATIONS; DiPaola JD, Yindee M, Plotnik JM (2020), Investigating the use of sensory information to detect and track prey by the Sunda pangolin (Manis javanica) with conservation in mind, Scientific Reports 10:9787, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-65898-x. A single subject failed a visual-only food-choice task; study discusses ecological/task limitations and semi-arboreal ecology. Does not establish eye regression, blindness, measured acuity or the exact burrowing class. Eye-state 1 and fossoriality 1 require further support; sensitivity-only treatment appropriate until resolved. Do not transfer retinal evidence from African pangolins.

light_detection: unknown (retinal projections to circadian nuclei present)
sources_and_qualifications: DIRECT SPECIES-MATCHED NEUROANATOMY; Autoradiographic study of the retinal projections in the Chinese pangolin, Manis pentadactyla (1991), Brain Behav Evol 37:104-110, https://doi.org/10.1159/000114351; PMID 2054583, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2054583/. Reports retinal projections to multiple visual and circadian nuclei; does not alone establish eye regression or poor acuity. Eye-state 1 remains unresolved under the current scale. Species-specific burrowing evidence and an explicit class boundary are still needed. Do not substitute cone-loss findings from Phataginus tricuspis.

eye_morphology_evidence: species-matched by explicit specimen provenance (Ganges-Brahmaputra system, Bangladesh); n = 1 juvenile (2 eyes): bulbus 4.0-4.5 mm; watch-glass-shaped lens with no non-nucleated fibres and a posterior capsule discontinuity; authors interpret the eye as 'embryonic rather than degenerate' (Dral & Beumer 1974). Both Platanista studies describe a markedly abnormal lens rather than unequivocal lens absence; a single juvenile cannot establish the lifelong developmental trajectory
image_forming_vision_evidence: not tested; retina 'quite well developed' with cone-only outer nuclear layer
sources_and_qualifications: UNVERIFIED IN FULL TEXT. Search located: a 1969 Science report that the rudimentary eye lacks a lens and may act as a light sensor (authors and specimen origin, Indus or Ganges, not inspected); Dral anatomical study of two eyes describing a watch-glass-shaped lens with a posterior capsule discontinuity, a well-developed retina and an 'embryonic rather than degenerate' eye (year and specimen origin not inspected; BioStor/BHL https://archive.org/download/biostor-182687/biostor-182687.pdf); Anderson (1878) monograph with an eye section (https://biodiversitylibrary.org/part/191305). Taxonomy: Indus and Ganges forms recognised as separate species, P. minor and P. gangetica, by Braulik et al. (2021), Marine Mammal Science (https://research-repository.st-andrews.ac.uk/handle/10023/21691); earlier studies refer to P. gangetica sensu lato, so their applicability to each species is UNRESOLVED unless the river system of the specimens is stated. 'Near-blind' descriptions are not used to code any variable. | SPECIMEN-ORIGIN CHECK (2 Nov 2026; full text not reachable). Dral ADG (1973?) The anatomy of the eye of the Ganges River Dolphin (German-English; Investigations on Cetacea, ed. G. Pilleri; citation details unverified). Search excerpts: watch-glass-shaped lens with capsule discontinuous at the posterior pole; anterior cell layer interpreted as a not fully atrophied vascular tunic; fairly well-developed retina whose outer nuclear layer contains only cone nuclei; eye 'embryonic rather than degenerate'. 'Ganges River Dolphin' was then the name of the whole genus and Pilleri's group also worked on Indus animals, so the title does not establish the river system; specimen origin UNVERIFIED. Secondary statements that Platanista lacks a lens (e.g. Guinness World Records) are not used for coding. | FULL TEXT READ (2 Nov 2026, PDF supplied by the authors): Dral ADG, Beumer L (1974) The anatomy of the eye of the Ganges River Dolphin Platanista gangetica (Roxburgh, 1801). Zeitschrift fur Saugetierkunde 39:143-167 (received 21 June 1973). Specimens: 'the eyes of a female Platanista gangetica, registered under nr. 16 in the University's collection' (University of Tokyo, courtesy M. Nishiwaki); 120.5 cm, juvenile (1-2 years); 'captured north of Tistamukh Ghat of Kola River, Bangla Desh, and transported alive to Japan'; died April 1970; eyes preserved in Zenker's fluid; serial sections, H.E., P.A.S., Azan; compared with Tursiops truncatus. Taxonomic applicability: Ganges-Brahmaputra system, i.e. P. gangetica in current taxonomy. Sample: one animal.

eye_morphology_evidence: probably species-matched (Indus): the animals studied are of Indus provenance; attribution of the anatomically examined eyes to those animals is implied ('our anatomical study'), not explicitly confirmed. Reported: vestigial eye not visible externally, concealed under skin with a small opening; flat cornea; 'degeneration and absorption of the lens fiber'; optic nerve of a few hundred fibres; pigment epithelium absent (Herald et al. 1969)
image_forming_vision: absent (the authors' anatomical inference, not a behavioural measurement)
image_forming_vision_evidence: Herald et al. 1969: 'incapable of forming a clear image on the retina because of the flat shape of the cornea and the absence of an effective lens'
light_detection_evidence: no response observed under the reported behavioural conditions; photoreceptive capacity suggested anatomically but not demonstrated (Herald et al. 1969). Neither observation establishes the opposite conclusion
sources_and_qualifications: As Platanista_gangetica. Elevated to species by Braulik et al. (2021) (https://research-repository.st-andrews.ac.uk/handle/10023/21691; type locality the Indus). Whether the 1969 lens report and the Dral study examined Indus specimens must be checked in the full texts before any code is assigned to this species. | SPECIMEN-ORIGIN CHECK (2 Nov 2026; full texts not reachable from the analysis environment: archive.org, biodiversitylibrary.org and digitalcommons.unl.edu blocked). Herald ER, Brownell RL Jr, Frye FL, Morris EJ, Evans WE, Scott AB (1969) Blind river dolphin: first side-swimming cetacean. Science 166:1408-1410. Abstract (as reproduced in the UNL repository record, https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/usdeptcommercepub/138): 'The rudimentary eye lacks the lens, but anatomical evidence suggests that the eye may serve as a light sensor.' Secondary accounts (Steinhart Aquarium history, https://www.dolphinproject.org/blog/the-captive-history-of-blind-river-dolphins/; zoo-history posts) state the study animals were three females flown from Sukkur, West Pakistan (Indus River), i.e. P. minor in current taxonomy. NOT YET VERIFIED in the full text: (i) that the eye anatomy was described from these Indus animals rather than other specimens; (ii) number of eyes examined. If (i) is confirmed, the 'lens absent' and 'possible light sensor' statements apply to P. minor (interpretation still required for coding). Conflicts with Dral (1973), see P. gangetica row; Dral's specimen origin not verified. | FULL TEXT READ (2 Nov 2026, PDF supplied by the authors): Herald ER, Brownell RL Jr, Frye FL, Morris EJ, Evans WE, Scott AB (1969) Science 166:1408-1410. Specimens: 'spent 11 days on the Indus River near Sukkur, 515 km north of Karachi, West Pakistan (November 1968)'; 'Three young females were taken' (4, 7 and 8 November; 121, 115 and 107 cm); obtained from Sindhi fishermen; survived 38, 24 and 44 days; skeletons CAS 14921, CAS 14922, MCZ 52306, described as 'the first from the Indus River'. Taxonomic applicability: Indus animals, i.e. P. minor (Braulik et al. 2021). The statement that Platanista 'lacked the crystalline lens' is attributed to Anderson (1878), not to this study. Sample: 3 juveniles; histological detail limited.

eye_morphology_evidence: direct: small eyes with permanently closed lids covered by skin; incomplete lens-fibre differentiation (PMC2587461); conversion to this category is an interpretation
image_forming_vision_evidence: retina with layers and cell types largely resembling mouse (PMC2871828) does not establish image formation
light_detection_evidence: direct: retained photo-avoidance response; thin, translucent skin over the eye (PMC3035857)
burrowing_ecology_evidence: secondary (species treatment, Handbook of the Mammals of the World via Plazi)
sources_and_qualifications: Species-matched primary studies located by search, full texts not yet inspected: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2587461 (eye and lens development; skin-covered eyes, incomplete lens-fibre differentiation, transparent cornea); https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2871828 (retina largely mouse-like; authors conclude the eyes were not lost on an evolutionary timescale); https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3035857 (no eyelids, unlike T. europaea; photo-avoidance retained). Authors and titles to be entered from the PMC records. Species treatment: https://treatment.plazi.org/GgServer/html/0380B547B64EFF9D9FAAF7D2FBFEC699.

eye_morphology_evidence: family-level statement only (small, not fur-covered eyes in Rhizomyinae)
sources_and_qualifications: No species-matched eye or vision study found. Family level: Animal Diversity Web, Rhizomyinae (https://animaldiversity.org/accounts/Rhizomyinae): small eyes not covered by fur; vision considered the least important sense (an interpretation by the account). Ecology: Thai National Parks species page (https://thainationalparks.com/species/hoary-bamboo-rat): solitary burrow with nest and latrine chambers; emerges at night to feed on bamboo and grasses. Eye states left unknown.
